title: Gospel of Mary

stories.title: 📜 Gospel of Mary
summaryBullets: Mary stands among the disciples and says, 'Do not remain in sorrow and doubt, for his grace will guide you and comfort you.' She encourages them to praise God and open their hearts to the Good.
She reminds them that what they seek is already living within them: '…the Child of Your True Humanity already lives within each one of you…'
crossRefs: John 14:27: Jesus leaves his peace with the disciples and tells them not to let their hearts be troubled or afraid, which is the comfort this text has Mary hand on in his absence.

Luke 24:36-43: The risen Jesus stands among them and says Peace to you, then answers their fright by showing his hands and feet and eating broiled fish in front of them, so the reassurance is given in a body they can touch.
John 20:11-18: Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus at the tomb and is sent to tell the disciples, the one place in the Gospels where a woman carries a message the men have not yet been given.
Luke 24:9-11: The women report the empty tomb to the eleven, who treat the account as idle talk and do not believe them, the same refusal this text stages between Andrew, Peter, Mary and Levi.
1 John 3:4: Sin is defined as lawlessness, the breaking of God's law, against this text's answer that there is no sin and that people make it themselves.
Romans 3:23: All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, stated as a fact about everyone rather than a category people invent by acting a certain way.

Acts 15:28-29: The Jerusalem council settles to lay on the Gentile believers no greater burden than a short list of necessary things, the nearest canonical parallel to the parting charge here against laying down rules.

Daniel 7:13-14: One like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and receives dominion and a kingdom that will not pass away, the passage standing behind the title this text renders as the Child of True Humanity.

translationNotes.note: The book survives chiefly in Papyrus Berolinensis 8502, a Coptic codex of the fifth century that Carl Reinhardt bought in Cairo in January 1896. A codex is a book of folded leaves stitched at the spine rather than a scroll. The Gospel of Mary stands first in it, on pages 1 to 19, and ten of those pages are gone: 1 to 6 and 11 to 14. That is why the text opens in the middle of a conversation already running and breaks off and restarts with nothing to bridge the gap.

The last stage of the Egyptian language, written in the Greek alphabet with a few extra letters kept from demotic. Two Greek scraps of this work also survive, both of the third century and both older than the Coptic: Papyrus Rylands 463, published by Colin Roberts in 1938, and Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 3525, published by Peter Parsons in 1983.

The title at the close of the Coptic uses the form used of the four Gospels, the Gospel according to Mary, and never says which one. She is given no father, no town and no family. Scripture names several: Mary Magdalene at Luke 8:2, Mary of Bethany at John 11:1, Mary the mother of James at Mark 16:1, and Mary the wife of Clopas at John 19:25.

translationNotes.original: Coptic: ⲡϣⲏⲣⲉ ⲙⲡⲣⲱⲙⲉ (pshere emprome) - Greek: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (ho huios tou anthropou)
translationNotes.note: The Coptic is literally the son of the man, the standard rendering of the Greek phrase the Gospels give as Son of Man. Some English versions of this book render it the Child of True Humanity to bring out humanity rather than a male child. Daniel 7:13 is where the title comes from, and Mark 14:62 has Jesus apply it to himself under oath before the high priest.

Favour freely given, and by extension the strength that favour supplies. The Coptic keeps the Greek word rather than translating it, as it does with much of its vocabulary. Ephesians 2:8-9 gives the canonical sense: saved by grace through faith, not of works, so that no one may boast.

The stuff the physical world is made of. The opening conversation asks whether matter will be destroyed and answers that all natures and all formed things exist in one another and will be resolved again into their own roots. Genesis 1:31 has God look at everything he had made and call it very good, and Colossians 1:16 has all things visible and invisible created by him.

The Saviour's answer in the opening conversation runs: there is no sin, but you make sin when you do the things that are like the nature of adultery, which is called sin. The canonical definitions run the other way. 1 John 3:4 makes sin lawlessness, the breaking of a standard that already exists. Romans 3:23 makes it universal. John 8:34 has Jesus call the one who commits sin a slave of sin.

Ruler. In the writings this shelf collects, the archons are rulers of the lower heavens who stop a rising soul and must be answered before it can pass. Mary's account has the soul challenged by Darkness, Desire and Ignorance, and then by a fourth with seven forms, among them the excitement of death, the kingdom of the flesh and the wrathful wisdom. The New Testament uses the same ordinary word of the ruler of this world at John 12:31 and of the rulers of this age at 1 Corinthians 2:6-8.

In ordinary Greek an age or a stretch of time, and that is all the New Testament means by it, as at Matthew 28:20, to the end of the age. In the systems behind the writings on this shelf an aeon is also a being, one of a set of divine emanations filling the upper world, and the two senses run together in the same sentence. A reader meeting the word has to work out which one is in play.

translationNotes.term: Where the mind is, there is the treasure
translationNotes.note: Nous is the mind, the faculty that perceives. The line is a deliberate turn on the canonical saying: Matthew 6:21 has Jesus say that where your treasure is, there your heart will be also, putting the treasure first and the heart after it. This text reverses the order and swaps heart for mind.

A term out of Greek philosophy for the highest reality and the proper goal of the mind, used here in places where a canonical text would say God. Mark 10:18 has Jesus answer the man who greets him as Good Teacher by asking why he calls him good, since no one is good except God alone.

The end of the soul's climb in this text is rest and silence. The word is the same one Jesus uses at Matthew 11:28-29, come to me and I will give you rest, and you will find rest for your souls, where the rest is given by a person rather than reached by an ascent. Hebrews 4:9-11 keeps a sabbath rest still ahead for the people of God.

Mark 2:14 names the man called from the tax booth as Levi son of Alphaeus, and Luke 5:27 tells the same call. He speaks last in this text and settles the dispute, telling Peter that if the Saviour made her worthy, Peter is not the one to reject her. Tax collectors worked as contractors for Rome and were despised for it, which is why the Gospels keep pairing the word with sinners.

translationNotes.term: Do not lay down any rules
translationNotes.note: The parting charge in this text is to lay down no rule beyond what was appointed and to give no law like a lawgiver, lest the giver be bound by it. Acts 15:28-29 has the Jerusalem council do exactly the opposite of nothing, issuing a short binding list to the Gentile churches. Matthew 28:19-20 has the risen Jesus command the nations be taught to observe all that he commanded.

The last surviving section has Andrew say he does not believe the Saviour said these things, and Peter ask whether he really spoke with a woman in private and without their knowledge. That objection has a canonical shape behind it: Luke 24:11 has the apostles hear the women's report from the tomb and treat it as idle talk.

stories.keyTakeaway: Mary comforts the grieving disciples, encourages inner peace, and points them to the living presence of the Savior within.

intro:
The Gospel of Mary carries its title at the close of the Coptic text, in the form used of the four Gospels: the Gospel according to Mary. It names no author, and it never says which Mary it means. She is given no patronymic, no town, and no family.

The text survives chiefly in one book, the Berlin Codex, catalogued as Papyrus Berolinensis 8502 and dated to the fifth century. Carl Reinhardt bought it in Cairo in January 1896. Besides the Gospel of Mary it carries the Apocryphon of John, the Sophia of Jesus Christ, and an epitome of the Act of Peter. The Gospel of Mary stands first in the codex, on pages 1 to 19, and ten of those nineteen pages are gone: pages 1 to 6 and pages 11 to 14. That is why the book opens in the middle of a conversation already under way, and why the account breaks off and picks up again several pages later with no way to close the gap. A reader who finds it starting and stopping without warning is reading exactly what survives.

Publication took nearly sixty years. Carl Schmidt had an edition of the Coptic all but printed in 1912 when a burst water pipe at the Leipzig printing house destroyed the entire run. Schmidt died in 1938. Walter Till took the work up in 1941, the war stopped it, and then the discovery at Nag Hammadi in 1945 of other copies of two texts in the same codex made it worth waiting for those to be published first. Till brought out the Berlin Codex in 1955.

Two small Greek fragments also survive, both of the third century and both older than the Coptic. Papyrus Rylands 463 was published by Colin Roberts in 1938. Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 3525, excavated by Grenfell and Hunt at Oxyrhynchus, was published by Peter Parsons in 1983.

What survives falls into two blocks separated by the second gap. The first is a conversation with the Saviour, on matter and on sin, ending with his departure and with Mary speaking to the disciples. The second is the close of Mary's report of what she saw, followed by a dispute among Andrew, Peter, Mary, and Levi over whether she is to be believed. The portion presented here is Mary's address to the disciples, telling them not to remain in grief and doubt.

No communion receives the Gospel of Mary as canonical. It stands in no canon list, no conciliar decree of Scripture, and no printed Bible of any tradition.
